beneficiaries_note: Our build: Club members and their families in the US (the youth centres on US military installations abroad serve US service families).
summary: Boys & Girls Clubs of America (BGCA) is the national organisation of about 1,000 local Club organisations, which run nearly 5,500 after-school and summer Clubs for 1.6 million members aged 5 to 18 and reach 2.57 million more children through outreach. In 2025 it spent $354 million on programmes: $213 million in grants to Clubs (two-thirds of it federal money passed through) and the rest on training, programme design, standards and help for new Clubs; all of it is modelled, as BGCA's share of the movement's member-years at the movement's cost per member, for 2025. Members' gains are built from the research on after-school programmes (no controlled evaluation of Clubs exists), valued by the adult earnings such gains predict (about 90% of the result), with the child care Clubs give parents (about 10%) and BGCA's advocacy for public funding as a small side effect; both branches are discounted for missing data. The result, about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.002 to 0.5), is low because the help goes to US families who consume around {{row:baseline_consumption}} a person a year, where on the site's log-income scale a dollar does far less than for a household on a few dollars a day, and a Club year costs about $1,700. The effect of a Club year on later earnings, the discount rate and the cost per member drive it.

rows.label: The movement's spending per member per year (local Clubs plus BGCA's own services)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: no movement-wide accounts are published. Anchors: Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston spent $31.5 million in the year to June 2023 (Form 990, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/42103922) for about 13,000 to 14,000 young people (bgcb.org): about $2,300 each in a high-cost city; Boys & Girls Clubs of the Valley (Arizona) spent 'more than $15 million' to serve '13,000+ K-12 youth' in 2020-21 (Arizona State University's economic impact report, https://www.bgcaz.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/ASU-Economic-Impact-Report-Underscores-Boys-Girls-Clubs-of-the-Valleys-Positive-Outcomes-on-Youth-Community-2022.pdf): about $1,150, in a pandemic year; and the movement's 81,100 professional staff (annual report p. 4), mostly part-time, at about $20,000 a year each, would cost about $1.6 billion, some 60% of a youth-service budget, so about $2.7 billion in all, $1,700 per member. The anchors are local spending only; BGCA's own services add about $86 a member ($138 million over 1.6 million). $1,700, from $950 to $2,900. It includes the outreach work (outreach_weight) and BGCA's own services, so BGCA's share of the movement's member-years is its spending over this.

rows.label: An outreach child's benefit as a share of a member's
rows.explainer: Our judgment: outreach is a sports league, a school-day session or an event, a few hours in the year against a member's 50-odd days. 3%, from 0 to 10%. Outreach counts only through this row; its cost is inside cost_per_member_year.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of BGCA's own services against a dollar the Clubs spend
rows.explainer: Our judgment, Convention 2 (credit by share of resources): BGCA's training, programme design, standards and help for new Clubs are part of the resources behind the movement's member-years, credited at the movement's average cost per member (1). The range is the doubt either way: national support is overhead to the Clubs and could do less than a dollar of Club staff time (0.4), or training and standards raise the quality of many Clubs' spending at once (1.5). No study measures it.

rows.label: Members whose Club year BGCA's 2025 spending pays for
rows.explainer: BGCA's grants and own services over the movement's spending per member: its share of the movement's members, by share of resources.

rows.label: People in a member's household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size, used by the parents' branch (members' families with children are larger; on the log scale for small amounts the size barely moves the result). The children's branch counts each child once (edu_children_reached): a child's earnings gain is their own, shared with the household later through the resource-sharing multiplier.

rows.label: People in the credited members' households
rows.explainer: Members' households times the US household size: the people the parents' branch counts.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: BGCA's full cost per person in the credited members' households, its own overhead included.

rows.label: Children's branch: children reached (member-years credited, outreach children at their weight)
rows.explainer: Members credited (one per member's household), plus the outreach children their spending also reaches (2.57 million for 1.6 million members) at their weight.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per person per year while the effect lasts (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: 0: no study of Clubs or after-school programmes measures life satisfaction. Children's social-emotional gains are in the effect size below, valued by the adult earnings they predict, so counting them as wellbeing too would count them twice.

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts
rows.explainer: Not used: the wellbeing branch is 0.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached, discounted
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Children: effect of a year's Club membership, in standard deviations of school and behaviour outcomes
rows.explainer: Our judgment, a blend of the after-school research. No controlled evaluation of Club membership exists; the effect is built from after-school programmes, the work Clubs do (Power Hour homework help, sports, arts, prevention programmes, mentoring). Durlak, Weissberg and Pachan's meta-analysis (American Journal of Community Psychology 2010, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10464-010-9300-6) finds 0.12 SD on grades and 0.17 on tests (Table 3) across 75 programmes, the effects in those using sequenced, active, focused and explicit (SAFE) skill training and the rest near zero; Kremer and others' Campbell-style meta-analysis of 24 studies with at-risk youth (Journal of Youth and Adolescence 2015, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-014-0226-4) finds 'Mean effects were small and non-significant for attendance and externalizing behaviors'; the national evaluation of 21st Century Community Learning Centers found no academic gains (James-Burdumy and others, Mathematica for the US Department of Education, 2005). Club-specific studies are non-experimental: Public/Private Ventures' 30-month study of teens (Arbreton and others, 'Making Every Day Count', 2009) links more frequent attendance with better outcomes. 0.09, between the null evaluations and Durlak's means; 0.02 to 0.2. How often members come is implementation_adj's question.

rows.label: Children: adult earnings gain per standard deviation of the childhood gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure for US youth programmes (Chetty, Friedman and Rockoff 2014): 10% (5% to 13%), below their 13% because much of the gain is social-emotional, which predicts earnings less than test gains.

rows.label: Children: years from a Club year to working age
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the members' ages (annual report p. 4): 41% aged 5 to 9, 29% 10 to 12, 18% 13 to 15, 8% 16 to 18; average about 10.5, so about 11 years to working age at about 22. From 8 to 15 years (work starting at 18 to 26). Every year is discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Children: ln(consumption) gain per member-year, all working years, discounted
rows.explainer: The proportional earnings gain on the log scale for each of the shared working years, discounted to the Club year at the shared rate and shared with the household (GiveWell's resource-sharing multiplier). A proportional gain is the same on the log scale whatever the adult's income. Taxes on the gain are not netted out.

rows.label: Parents: average weekly fee of an after-school programme, 2020 (US$)

source.title: Afterschool Alliance, America After 3PM 2020, national fact sheet
source.quote: $99.40 average weekly cost of afterschool programs, among parents who report that they pay a fee

rows.explainer: What parents who pay for after-school care pay per week, from the national household survey of 31,000 families. The same survey: 78% of parents of children in programmes agree that the programme helps them keep their job.

rows.label: Parents: weeks a year of Club care
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the school year's 36 weeks after school plus part of the summer, when many Clubs run full-day camps. 42, from 36 to 50.

rows.label: Parents: share of that price that is a real gain to the family
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the counterfactual of this branch (asked here only): families who would otherwise pay for care save the fee less the Club's own small one (most Clubs charge $0 to $50 a year: Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston waives it for 2025-26); families whose child would otherwise be home alone, with relatives or in a free school programme gain supervision and time they value below the market price. 30%, from 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Parents: value of a member's year of Club care to the family (US$, 2025 prices)
rows.explainer: The weekly price in 2025 dollars, times the weeks, times how often the member comes, times the share that is a real gain.

rows.label: Parents: value of the year's Club care per household member (US$)
rows.explainer: The child-care value spread over the household. The children's own gain is the earnings branch, a different change for different people.

rows.label: Average consumption per person in the country by the household survey (US$)
rows.explainer: The Consumer Expenditure Survey's consumption per person, 2024, in the same dollars as the value (2025's price change is small).

rows.label: Anchor: consumption per person of the poorest fifth of US households, as a share of the average person's
rows.explainer: Context: the poorest fifth spend 45% of the average household's (BLS 2024), in households of 1.6 people against 2.4: per person 0.67 of the average.

rows.label: Members' families' consumption per person relative to the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 63% of members live in households that qualify for free or reduced-price school lunch (annual report p. 4), under 185% of the poverty line, and families with children consume less per person than the average; the rest are near-poor and middle-income. 1.1 of the poorest fifth's 0.67 (0.74 of the average person's), from 0.82 to 1.4.

rows.label: The people served's consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: The anchor times the judgment above.

Years the help keeps its money value for the people served

rows.label: Parents: ln(consumption) gain per household member from a member's year of care
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the clients' own consumption: a dollar does far less for a US household than for one living on a few dollars a day.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0 in the main chain: Clubs' health outcomes (physical activity, meals, substance use) have no controlled evidence of their own; they are in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: no study finds deaths averted by after-school programmes; violence prevention is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Context, at zero weight while no deaths are counted (deaths_averted_per_person is 0): the members' ages, 5 to 18, so the chain stays complete.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Context, at zero weight while no deaths are counted (deaths_averted_per_person is 0): the members' ages, 5 to 18, so the chain stays complete.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Context, at zero weight while no deaths are counted (deaths_averted_per_person is 0): the members' ages, 5 to 18, so the chain stays complete.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (validity of the after-school literature for the children's branch), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment on the internal validity of the literature chain: Durlak and others' meta-analysis draws on many small, published evaluations, where publication bias and self-reported outcomes inflate effects; the large null evaluations (21st Century Community Learning Centers, Kremer and others) are already in the effect's range. Two doubts are counted elsewhere, once each: social-emotional gains predicting earnings less (the shared earnings figure) and whether members come as often as the studies' participants (implementation_adj). The parents' branch is at face value (its doubt is cc_value_share). 0.85, from 0.65 to 1.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the effect is against control groups whose children did what they would otherwise do, other programmes included; the parents' counterfactual is in cc_value_share. BGCA's money could be replaced by others: leverage_funging_adj.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the movement's paid spending (in cost_per_member_year) over all resources behind the member-years, volunteers' hours at the US value of a volunteer hour and donated space added. Grants from government and other funders to Clubs are in the paid spending and already shared through the cost per member.

rows.label: Club volunteers in 2025

source.title: Boys & Girls Clubs of America, 2025 Annual Report
source.page: p. 4, About Our Club Kids & Staff

rows.explainer: Unpaid adults who coach, tutor and mentor at Clubs.

rows.label: Hours a year per volunteer
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most Club volunteers coach a season or help at events; mentors give an hour a week. 30, from 10 to 80.

rows.label: Donated space and other in-kind help, as a share of the movement's spending
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 2,650 of the 5,500 Club sites are in schools and 210 in public housing (annual report p. 3), usually rent-free; 480 are military youth centres run on bases. 5%, from 0 to 15%.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (how often members come, against the studies' participants)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: an average member attends about 28% of weekdays (attendance_share, about 1.4 days a week); participants in the after-school studies typically attended two to three days a week, and the Club-specific studies (Arbreton and others 2009; Anderson-Butcher and others 2003) find outcomes rise with attendance, a dose-response. 0.7, from 0.4 to 1. Applied to the children's branch; the parents' branch already counts attendance.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Clubs make up part of a lost BGCA grant from local donors and other funders (Andreoni and Payne 2011 on how charities fundraise around grants); about two-thirds of BGCA's grants are restricted federal money passed through, which Clubs could not easily replace: 0.9, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): BGCA has no controlled evaluation of Club membership, its reach per dollar is a judged cost per member, and the effect comes from the research on after-school programmes. Both branches take the shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Parents' branch: all adjustments
Children's branch: units of value before adjustments
Parents' branch: units of value before adjustments
All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the two branches' adjustments, for reading only (Convention 4).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, effects not modelled, each with its sign: less crime and violence among members beyond their own earnings (+; Schinke, Orlandi and Cole 1992, Journal of Community Psychology, found less drug activity and vandalism in public-housing estates with a new Club, a quasi-experiment, while Kremer and others 2015 find no significant effect on externalising behaviour); meals and snacks (+, mostly paid by the federal child nutrition programme), physical activity and substance-use prevention (+; Clubs' SMART Moves programme); teen pregnancy prevention (+); parents' extra earnings beyond the care's price (+, small at the log scale); members drawn from other youth programmes of similar value (−, partly in the effect's control groups already). +10%, from −5% to +30%.

rows.label: BGCA's advocacy for public funding of Clubs, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: Our judgment of what BGCA's advocacy adds, net of its cost to taxpayers. BGCA counts $406.1 million of public funding for Clubs in 2025 ($327.5 million won by state alliances of Clubs, $76.4 million by Clubs with BGCA's help, $2.2 million federal; annual report p. 4), from about $3 million of its own advocacy (facts/boys_girls_clubs_of_america.json; its Form 990 lobbying was $603,556 in 2024). The federal grants it passes through are in the grants branch, not here. Most such money recurs each year and would mostly come anyway (Baumgartner and others, Lobbying and Policy Change, 2009: resources explain little of who wins; our judgment, about 15% of a coalition's money is its doing) and BGCA is one of several parties (the state alliances, Clubs, their boards): perhaps 15% × 30% × $406 million = about $18 million of extra public money for Clubs, six times its advocacy cost. But public money isn't free: on the site's log-income scale a dollar taken from taxpayers costs about 1.2 ÷ $58,500 of ln(consumption), while a Club dollar gains members and parents only a little more, after this model's adjustments, than it costs, so the net is small and could be below zero. Worked through: $18 million is about 5% of BGCA's cost; a Club dollar gains about 4.3e-5 of ln(consumption) after this model's adjustments, against about 2e-5 for the taxpayer (1.2 ÷ (1.05 × $58,517), the cost of public funds and payer multiple), so about 55% of its value is net: 5% × 55% ≈ +3%, from −2% to +10%: a side effect, added to the modelled value. It is not a separate past-average model because its cost is under 1% of BGCA's spending and its net value near zero.
